title: TB9-13616
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): XXXX XXXX XXXX (Principal Appellant) and her daughter, XXXX XXXX XXXX (Associate Appellant), citizens of Nigeria, appeal a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD), dated May 15, 2019, rejecting their claims for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX (Principal Appellant) and her daughter, XXXX XXXX XXXX (Associate Appellant), citizens of Nigeria, appeal a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD), dated May 15, 2019, rejecting their claims for refugee protection.

The Appellants' allegations are as follows. The Principal Appellant's (PA) husband was killed by gunmen on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2017, and the Appellants were abducted, on behalf of the husband's brother. A few days later, the husband's brother approached the PA and told her that the PA's children had to leave, that he would be appropriating the family property and marrying the PA. He threatened that if the PA and her children did not comply, he would kill them. The Appellants hid at a church. Thereafter, they fled Nigeria on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2017, and traveled to the United States (US). They arrived in Canada on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2017 and applied for refugee protection on September 13, 2017.

The Appellants' hearing was on May 9, 2019, and their claims were rejected on May 15, 2019 on the basis of credibility. The Appellants appeal to the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD). The Appellants do not submit new evidence or request an oral hearing.
I dismiss the appeal. The RPD was correct in finding that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.
My role is to look at all the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.1
In my analysis, I have considered Guideline 4: Women Refugee Claimants Fearing Gender-Related Persecution.2

The Appellants argue that the RPD erred in the following findings: a. Misinterpreting the Appellants' evidence that they were receiving threats from the PA's brother-in-law when in hiding3 b. Mischaracterizing the PA's evidence regarding her application for a US visa4 c. Unreasonably impugning the PA's credibility regarding her delay in leaving Nigeria5 d. Concluding that the Appellants were asylum-shopping and discrediting the PA's evidence by ignoring the harsh and punitive plight of asylum seekers in the US6 e. Misunderstanding and mischaracterizing the PA's evidence regarding Ibadan as an IFA7 f. Unreasonably impeaching the police report8 g. Generally discounting the Appellants' other corroborating documents.9 Narrative is inconsistent regarding whether the Appellants were threatened while in hiding

The RPD decision drew a negative credibility inference on the basis of an internal inconsistency in the Appellants' Basis of Claim (BOC) amended narrative.10 Specifically, the RPD decision states that the Appellants' amended narrative indicates that they were in hiding from the brother-in-law from XXXX XXXX XXXX 2017, until they left Nigeria on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2017. However, the RPD also noted that the amended narrative simultaneously indicates that, during this time, the Appellants were still receiving threats from the brother-in-law. The RPD asked the PA how it was possible that they could still be getting threats from the brother-in-law if they were in hiding. The PA responded that she mixed up the facts due to trauma. The RPD did not accept the PA's explanation. The Appellants argue in this appeal that the ongoing threats while they were in hiding was by virtue of the brother-in-law going to visit their house, rather than threatening them personally.11 Based on my independent assessment, I do not find that the RPD erred, for the following reasons.

First, the Appellants submit that paragraphs 11, 12, 13, and 16 of their amended Basis of Claim narrative repeatedly states that the threats to them were continuous. The Appellants therefore dispute the RPD's finding that their narrative is inconsistent. However, I note that the RPD's concern pertains to whether the Appellants were threatened by the brother-in-law after they went in hiding. Contrarily, paragraphs 11, 12 and 13 in the amended narrative12 only refer to threats before the Appellants went into hiding. Specifically, the narrative is written chronologically and paragraphs 11, 12, and 13 appear before any reference to the Appellant's going into hiding, which is not mentioned until paragraphs 16 and 17 of the amended narrative. Therefore, I do not find that the references to ongoing threats in paragraphs 11, 12 and 13 address the issue of how the Appellants could have been threatened by the brother-in-law when they were hidden from him.

Paragraph 16 of the amended narrative states that the Appellants made plans to go to the US because they continued to be threatened by the brother-in-law and they already had US visas. The Appellants were asked when they decided to leave the country, and they responded that they left in XXXX.13 Therefore, this suggests that the Appellants continued to be threatened by the brother-in-law until XXXX even though they were actually hidden from him in the preceding few months, and since XXXX XXXX The Appellants explain that what they meant in terms of the ongoing threats while they were in hiding was that the brother-in-law had been visiting their vacant home. However, based on my independent assessment, I do not find, on a balance of probabilities, that this is the case, for the following reasons.

First, the narratives do not state that the brother-in-law continued to threaten them by repeatedly attending at their house. The threats are a central aspect of their claims and the Appellants had the opportunity to add this important detail to any of the three versions of their narratives,14 but did not. Secondly, when the PA was asked how it was possible that they were being threatened by the brother-in-law if they were in hiding, she did not state that it was because he was going to their house. Rather, the PA gave no explanation and said it was an error. It was only at almost the very end of the hearing, and in questioning from counsel to the Associate Appellant (AA), that the AA contradicted her mother by saying that when they would go to check on their house that the neighbours informed them that the brother-in-law came again and "said this or said that."15 However, the Appellants have not provided any corroboration from any neighbours on this point notwithstanding that they did produce an affidavit from a neighbour.

Overall, based on the foregoing, I do not accept the Appellants' argument that the reference to ongoing threats in paragraph 16 of their amended narrative were because the brother-in-law was visiting their house. I agree with the RPD that the narrative is internally inconsistent, and that the AA's explanation was an attempt to reconcile this inconsistency, although this is not central.

Regarding the PA's explanation that this inconsistency was due to past trauma, I do not accept this explanation. As the RPD noted, the original and amended narrative were written by the AA, not the PA. Also, there is no evidence that the PA suffers from psychological symptoms that affected her ability to testify. Finally, having listened to the audio recording of the hearing, I also do not find that the PA had any obvious or apparent difficulty with testifying either. PA's evidence regarding why she applied for a US visa undermines credibility

The Appellants submit that the RPD erred by drawing a negative credibility inference regarding the PA's testimony over why she applied for a US visa.16 Based on my independent assessment, I do not find that the RPD erred, for the following reasons.

The RPD asked the PA why she had a US visa in the first place.17 The PA responded that it was to get protection. The RPD put to the Appellant if she was saying that she got a US visa in order to flee her brother-in-law. The PA very cleared confirmed "yes," in English. The RPD then put to the PA that her visa was issued in XXXX 2016, and that this was before the alleged persecution. At this point, the PA's evidence changed to say that she wanted to come to the US for medical reasons and that her husband had relatives in the US who were going to take care of her. Her counsel also interjected to assert that it was the PA's initial response that she meant protection for health reasons, not protection from her brother-in-law. However, I have listened to the audio and can confirm that the Appellant only raised the prospect of health treatment after the inconsistency was put to her by the RPD.

I do not accept the Appellants' submission in this appeal that the PA had initially misunderstood the question and clarified her response once she understood. The RPD's question was clear and the Appellant's response was confirmed before the inconsistency was put to her. It was only at this point that the PA's testimony evolved. Furthermore, at the outset of the hearing the Appellants were instructed to state if they did not understand a question, but the PA made no such suggestion after the inconsistency was raised to her. I find that the Appellants' submission that the PA did not understand the question is an attempt to rectify her testimony at the hearing. I therefore draw a negative credibility inference from the PA's evolving evidence regarding why she obtained a US visa and find that this undermines the Appellants allegations of persecution and overall credibility. Appellants' delay in leaving Nigeria undermines credibility

The RPD drew a negative credibility inference from the Appellants' delay in leaving Nigeria.18 Specifically, although the alleged threats initially took place in XXXX 2017, the Appellants did not leave Nigeria until XXXX 2017, notwithstanding that they had valid US visas throughout. The Appellants submit that the RPD erred in rejecting the PA's testimony that the delay was because she needed time to rehabilitate before traveling. The Appellants' also now submit in this appeal that the delay was because of financial and logistical reasons.19 Based on my independent assessment, I do not find that the RPD erred, for the following reasons.

The RPD asked the PA why the Appellants did not leave Nigeria until XXXX XXXX.20 I have listened to the audio recording of the hearing and note that the PA responded that she wanted to get some rest, make sure she was sound and put herself together before making a trip. I therefore find that it was not the PA's evidence that the delay in leaving was due to finances or logistics. The RPD then asked the PA that if her life was in danger, why would she remain at the church for three months. The PA explained that she was not sure what her brother-in-law was capable of doing. I do not accept the PA's testimony that she was not sure what her brother-in-law was capable of doing. It is the Appellants' evidence that he ordered the murder of her husband and abduction of herself and her children and threatened to kill her and her children. I do not find it is credible that in the face of such danger, the Appellants would bide their time. While I acknowledge that a relocation to a foreign country is no small feat, I do not find that living under the threat of death can be explained by virtue of wanting time to rest first. Therefore, I do not accept that the PA's testimony adequately explains their failure to leave Nigeria earlier, and I further find that the delay demonstrates a lack of subjective fear. I find that the RPD did not err in drawing a negative credibility inference in this regard. Failure to claim in the US undermines subjective fear and credibility

The RPD found that the Appellants never intended to seek protection in the US and that the Appellants were asylum shopping.21 Specifically, the RPD did not accept the PA's testimony that, when they arrived in the US, they were turned away from her husband's relative, and accordingly proceeded to Canada because of President Trump's anti-refugee views. The Appellants argue that the RPD unreasonably ignored the objective evidence on the "harsh and punitive plight of asylum seekers in the US".22

Based on my independent assessment, I find that the Appellants' actions undermine that they subjectively feared persecution, and that it was always their intention to relocate to Canada. Specifically, I note that, until she fled, the PA had never been outside Nigeria her entire life,23 yet she nevertheless previously applied for and sought entry into Canada, but was denied a Canadian visa.24 Furthermore, even though the Appellants have relatives in the US and were legally there under a valid visa, they only remained in the US for one week before proceeding to Canada. I note the PA's explanation that they did not stay in the US because they were allegedly turned away by her husband's American relatives for unknown reasons.25 However, I do not accept this explanation. The PA testified earlier that she had obtained a US visa in order to visit her husband's relatives in the US because they would take care of her.26 However, the PA subsequently testified that when they arrived in the US, the relatives told them they could not stay with them and that they should go elsewhere. Additionally, the PA's testimony indicates that it was only after pleading with the relatives for help that the relatives recommended that the Appellants proceed to Canada because of Trump. Therefore, the advice to proceed to Canada was not borne out of a desire to help the Appellants but, rather, to be rid of them. I find that the PA's testimony that they left the US because the relatives did not want to help her is inconsistent with the PA's earlier testimony that she planned to go to the US because the relatives would help her. I therefore find that the Appellants had a pre-meditated plan to relocate to Canada, and that this undermines their subjective fear. I also note that the Federal Court has recently found that the lack of effort to file an asylum claim in the US combined with the fact that a claimant had previously been denied a Canadian visa can be indicative of a lack of subjective fear of persecution.27 PA's evidence regarding Ibadan as an IFA undermines her credibility

The RPD decision states that the PA testified that she could relocate to Ibadan, but when she was asked for further clarification, she changed her evidence.28 The RPD drew a negative credibility inference as a result. The Appellants argue that the PA misunderstood the question and that the RPD displayed zeal to discredit and disbelieve her.29 Based on my independent assessment, I do not find that the RPD erred in concluding that the PA contradicted her own testimony and that this undermines her credibility.

Having listened to the audio recording of the hearing, the exchange can be summarized as follows.30 - RPD asks the PA if there was anywhere, she could go in Nigeria to be safe from her brother-in-law. o PA responds that Ibadan is the only place she could go for protection but that it's possible that he could trace them there since it's only one hour away from their property. In other places in Nigeria they will be viewed as prostitutes because they are female. Also, there is too much uncertainty in Nigeria, she does not know where to settle and felt traumatized. - RPD confirms to PA that her evidence is that she could go to Ibadan. o PA responds that she cannot go to Ibadan because her brother-in-law could find her there since he is a politician. - RPD reiterates to PA that she said she could go to Ibadan. o PA responds that it is the only place she could go back that is the only environment she could comfortably fit into based on her background. She does not know anyone in other places in Nigeria. - RPD confirms to PA that her evidence is that she could fit into Ibadan because of her background. o PA repeats that her brother-in-law would look for her anywhere she is. - Counsel interjects at this point to clarify and instruct the PA regarding the RPD's question. That what is in Ibadan that is compatible with her background. - RPD again asks PA why she would be comfortable because of her background in Ibadan o PA states that she was only looking at the possibility that it is close, but that she cannot live in Ibadan. - RPD reiterates to PA her evidence that she said she would be comfortable in Ibadan because of her background. o PA responds "no."

Based on the foregoing, I accept that the PA consistently testified that she would not be safe in Ibadan because her brother-in-law could find her. However, with regards to reasonableness of Ibadan, the gist of the PA's responses was that, based on her background, she would be comfortable living in Ibadan. The PA specifically stated that elsewhere she does not know anyone, and the Appellants may be viewed as prostitutes because they are female. I therefore find, based on her testimony, that the PA understood what information was being solicited from her, and that she effectively testified that Ibadan was a reasonable option for relocation. However, on the basis that she then recanted her testimony, I find that the PA demonstrated once more that she is willing to contradict and change her evidence to rectify shortcomings in her initial responses. I therefore find that the PA is not a credible witness and that this undermines the Appellant's overall credibility. Substance of police report undermines Appellants' credibility

The RPD decision did not find the police report to be credible on the basis that it does not refer to a central allegation, which is that the Appellants' had been abducted.31 The Appellants' submit that such information is missing from the report because the police in Nigeria are ill-trained, inefficient, ill-equipped and ineffective, and that the RPD erred by relying on what the report does not say.32 Based on my independent assessment, I give the police report little weight, for the following reasons.

Having listened to the audio recording of the hearing, I note that the RPD raised at the hearing to the AA that the police report does not mention the abduction of the Appellants, which is an important event.33 The AA responded that the abduction is not mentioned because police do not write much in the police reports, just the fact of the death. I acknowledge that evidence from a third party cannot be judged for what it does not say and that the police force in Nigeria may be ineffective. However, based on my independent review of the police report, I do not find that the failure to mention the abduction is due to shortcomings in the police force. Specifically, I note that the language in the police report is simply a copy of an Affidavit authored by the AA herself dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 2017.34 As it is the AA's own affidavit that is the source of the language in the alleged police report, I find that the AA's failure to mention the abduction in her own Affidavit undermines the credibility of the allegations of persecution.

Overall, as the contents of the police report is from the AA's affidavit, which is her own document, I find that the lack of any mention of the abduction in these documents undermines the credibility of the Appellants allegations of persecution. Remaining corroborative evidence does not outweigh negative credibility findings

The RPD determined that, with respect to the Appellants' remaining corroborative evidence including the neighbour's affidavit, the husband's death certificate and letter from the church, this evidence does not outweigh its overall credibility concerns.35 The Appellants submit that the RPD failed to independently and engagingly consider the corroborating documents.36 Based on my independent assessment, I do not find that the RPD erred, for the following reasons.

First, the caselaw states that a lack of credibility concerning central elements can extend to other elements of a claim and the documentary evidence.37 Here, the RPD correctly found that the Appellants were not credible before extending this finding to the corroborating evidence. I further note that the RPD decision indicates that it did consider the remaining documents before concluding that they did not outweigh its credibility concerns. Therefore, as the RPD did review all the corroborative evidence, I do not find that that the RPD erred simply because it did not explicitly discuss each particular document in its decision.38

Furthermore, even if the RPD erred by not assessing each particular document in its decision, based on my independent assessment, I do not find that the Appellants' corroborating documents outweigh the finding that their allegations of persecution are not credible, for the following reasons.

I have already considered the police report and the AA's affidavit in my analysis. I find that these are not credible because these documents are based on the AA's self-report, and I have concerns with the Appellants' credibility, as outlined above.
Regarding the husband's death certificate, I do not find this to be probative because the certificate does not describe the cause of death, or state that he died from gunshot wounds.39

Regarding the neighbour's affidavit,40 the most relevant parts of the affidavit, which pertain to the murder and abduction, and which also form the bulk of the affidavit [paragraphs 7(a)-(i)], is information that was relayed by the AA to the Affiant, and is therefore not within the Affiant's personal knowledge. The remaining information in the affidavit is also scant, alleging that the neighbour heard a noise and the following day saw blood in the Appellants' apartment. While I recognize that generally documents from non-parties ought to be analysed on the basis of the information they contain, I assign this affidavit little weight on the basis that the majority of its content was informed by the AA and lacks sufficiency of other information.41
Finally, I give the Church letter42 limited weight on the basis that the allegations in it that the PA's husband was murdered are not based on the Reverend's personal knowledge.

Overall, I find that the Appellants are not credible and have not credibly established, on a balance of probabilities, that they are being persecuted by the PA's brother-in-law. I find that the Appellants do not face a serious possibility of persecution in Nigeria, and that, on a balance of probabilities, that they would not be personally subjected to a danger of torture or face a risk to life, or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment in Nigeria.

Pursuant to s.111(1)(a) of the IRPA, I dismiss the appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection. (signed) K.
